samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A is a clean table sorted with the most overdue first. Its 'Overdue N days' labels make status clear in words, and amounts sit in one column aligned on the decimal point under a ($) header. It also splits the part-paid invoice into Total, Received and Balance due. B also sorts and labels status well and shows the part-paid balance, but it uses cards: dates are folded into text lines rather than their own columns, amounts repeat the $ on every row, and the list runs below the fold, so it is harder to scan at a glance. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B uses a proper table, with right-aligned amounts in separate Total, Received and Balance columns, the currency stated in the headers, and dates in their own column. Overdue rows get text labels and are sorted most overdue first. A sorts and labels well, and it shows the part-paid balance clearly. But A's card layout puts dates inline with other text and spreads amounts across cards, so they don't line up as a column, and the page runs past one screen.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both pages sort the invoices by due date, leave out paid ones, label overdue rows in words, and show the $750.00 still owed on the part-paid invoice. A has the edge: it gives the currency once in the headers, shows the $400.00 received in its own column, and adds a total-owed row. B repeats the $ sign on every row and tucks the payment received into a subtitle line. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both pages list the same six unpaid invoices with the most overdue first. Both label overdue rows in words and correctly show $750.00 still owed on #1044. B is slightly better: it states the currency once in the column headers, gives the $400.00 received its own column and adds a total row, while A repeats the $ sign in every row. B's overdue labels also add an icon, so they rely less on color.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both pages show only the unpaid invoices, most overdue first, label each status in words, and correctly show $750.00 still owed on the part-paid invoice. B scores higher because it adds separate Invoice total and Received columns with right-aligned figures and a totals row, and states the currency once in the headers. A uses a consistent $ on every amount but tucks the issue dates into a subline instead of a column, and B's wrapped customer name is only a small flaw. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both pages show only unpaid invoices, put the most overdue first, show a text label for each status and give the part-paid balance of $750.00. A has separate right-aligned columns for invoice total, received and balance due, with the $ stated once in each header, plus a totals row, so the part payment is easier to check. B is a clean dark design, but it puts issue dates and invoice totals in a small subtitle line instead of their own columns, which makes them harder to scan.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers get every per-row and total figure right ($13.33/$10.01/$250.00/$12.50, $4,250.50, 199, $21.36, 3.6% from 187 ÷ 5,220). samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers reject the table for the right reason and give a scannable list without changing what the rules mean. B's example of when a table would fit is more on point: rules that each carry the same extra facts, such as a contact or a penalty. Its grouped headings also make the list easier to scan. A's example (plot sizes, fees, opening hours) is less relevant to rules, and its tip to 'pair the gate code with a date' is unclear. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend a list over a table, explain why a table doesn't fit, avoid made-up columns, and show the rules laid out. A does better on criterion 3: it says a table would make sense if each rule gained the same extra details, such as a contact or a consequence. B only mentions unrelated data like fees and opening hours. B's bold lead words are a clean way to make the list scannable, but its trailing list of optional tweaks drifts toward surveying options, and the gate-code tweak is muddled.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers advise against a table and suggest a scannable list without changing what the rules mean. A gives the clearer reason (a table suits rows that share the same attributes) and uses bold lead words, which handles seven rules without the somewhat forced groupings B uses, such as putting the gate code under 'Tools and site'. B does better on when a table would fit, naming concrete extra columns like a contact or a consequence, but A is slightly stronger overall. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers advise against a table and explain why: the rules are single sentences, so there is nothing for extra columns. B explains this a little more clearly by naming when a table does work (rows that share attributes, like a price list) and gives a tidy list with bold lead words that keeps each rule's meaning. A's grouped headings also work, but its groups are a bit arbitrary (watering filed with plots, the gate code with tools) and it offers more optional suggestions, so it reads slightly less decisive.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers turn down the table for the right reason, warn about how tables display on phones, and show a clean list. B edges ahead: its bold lead words on every bullet make the list easy to scan, it commits to one layout, and it adds a useful gate-code callout. A recommends headings and then calls them optional at seven rules, which weakens its own advice. B reworded two rules, but it says so and the meaning doesn't change. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend a list, explain clearly why a table would leave a single real column, and avoid inventing columns. A's bold lead-in words make each rule easy to find while keeping the list flat, and it says openly where it reworded lines. B's headed groups are a bit arbitrary (one group holds a single rule), though it keeps the rules exactly as written, and A's optional grouping idea slightly misplaces the herb bed.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick stacked cards, keep the desktop table for dispatchers, and add search, so they agree on the main approach. B orders the fields a little better for a rep on a call, putting items last and total/tracking higher, while A puts the items text above total and tracking. A wins on items 4 and 5: every value keeps its label on the card, the total is right-aligned with consistent decimals, and tracking has a Copy button. B's cards drop the labels ("Oct 9 · $84.20"), and A's implementation notes (a `<dl>`, `display: none`, screen-reader concerns) are more concrete. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend stacked cards with sticky search and keep the desktop table, so they are close. B does better on rubric item 4: Total and Tracking keep their labels, the total is right-aligned with the same decimals on every card, and the tracking number has a copy button that is easy to hit. B also gives an accessibility reason for its implementation. A's field order better matches what a rep needs on a call (items last, with a clear reason, and tracking links to the carrier), but A drops labels on the card and puts the total inline with the date.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend stacked cards with the same field order, keep the desktop table, and add a sticky search. B does better on rubric item 4: it labels date, total and tracking, keeps tracking on one line, and explains why it renders a separate card list (restyled table cells cause screen-reader problems). A puts date, total and ship method on one muted line with no labels, but it is stronger on making tracking tappable, since tapping the number opens the carrier's page. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend the same stacked-card layout, keep the desktop table and open with search, so they are close. A is better on item 4: every value keeps its label ('Placed', 'Total', 'Tracking'), and status is shown as a word, not by color alone. B squeezes date, total and ship method into one unlabeled muted line, though B is stronger on making the tracking number tappable to the carrier page and on weighing the two ways to build it.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers commit to one phone layout, keep the dispatcher table and add a pinned search box. A is stronger on presentation details: labels travel with the values, the total uses right-aligned tabular figures with the currency named, tracking has a copy button and carrier link, and it gives a concrete implementation route (restyle the real table under 640px with an aria-expanded button). B gives tracking more visual priority without a tap, but its cards rely on implied rather than explicit labels and its implementation guidance is thinner. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick one concrete phone layout and keep the desktop table for dispatchers. B does better on labeling (label and value pairs, tabular figures for the total, a copy button for tracking) and gives a clearer implementation route (restyle the real table below about 640px, use aria-expanded). B's weak spot is putting tracking behind a tap, though it flags that and offers to swap it in. A keeps tracking visible on every card but leaves the total without a label and says less about how to build it.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B explains the cause clearly, gives a precision choice with its tradeoff, moves km into the header, and lists the fixes in order of impact with sensible caveats about the font. A contradicts itself: it first says Verdana uses proportional digits, then says Verdana has tabular figures by default. It also lists the font fix before the decimal fix it calls more important, and treats moving the unit to the header as an optional afterthought while its example output still has km in every cell. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A explains the cause clearly, puts the fixes in order of impact (consistent decimals, then the unit moved to the heading, then tabular-nums) and is careful about what it doesn't know regarding Trebuchet MS. Answer B contradicts itself: it first says Verdana uses proportional figures, then says Verdana's digits are tabular by default. It also puts the font fix first while calling decimals the bigger problem, keeps 'km' in every cell of its example, and treats moving the unit to the heading as optional.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers diagnose the problem correctly. A is tighter and ordered by impact: it treats moving the unit into the header as a core fix and gives a clear choice between 1 and 3 decimals. However, A states as fact that both fonts have fixed-width digits and calls tabular-nums a 'guarantee', which overclaims. B is more careful about the font and says tabular-nums only works if the font has those figures. But B makes moving the unit optional, offers a fiddly span workaround instead, and is inconsistent about precision: its code and HTML use 2 decimals while its advice and final example use 3. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B lists all three fixes in order of impact, makes moving the unit into the header a core step, and gives a clear choice of decimals with what each option costs. A diagnoses the problem well and is more careful about the font, but it treats moving the unit as optional and suggests a workaround. A's code example also uses 2 decimals while its final display uses 3. B's claim that Trebuchet MS and Verdana normally have fixed-width digits is somewhat confident, and it never says tabular-nums only works if the font has tabular figures.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly diagnose the mixed decimal places and recommend formatting to 3 decimals. A also treats moving the unit to the header as a core fix, and it speaks conditionally about whether Trebuchet MS has tabular figures, noting that tabular-nums only works if the font supports it. B makes moving 'km' optional and states flatly that the font isn't the cause. It also overclaims that tabular-nums guarantees equal digit widths whatever the fallback font. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B gives the full diagnosis (mixed decimals plus a unit in every cell), moves km into the header as a firm step, and correctly says tabular-nums only works if the font supports it, without asserting what Trebuchet does. A diagnoses well and fixes the precision, but makes moving the unit optional, says the font isn't the cause, and claims tabular-nums 'guarantees' equal digit widths with no note that the font must support them. B is a little longer, and its system-ui suggestion is weak, but it fits the rubric better.
